title: Solve It, Estimate It and The Last S'more
goal: I can find the clue word, add or subtract, estimate to check, and tell the lesson a story teaches.

card.desc: Welcome back! You start with a quick review of Weeks 1–3. Then you find the clue words that tell you to add or subtract, estimate by rounding to the nearest hundred, and check if an answer is reasonable. In reading, you go back to Theo's campfire for “The Last S'more” and find the theme, the lesson a story teaches (Pathways Week 4).

win: Clue words, estimates and themes: you came back strong! 🔥

slides.title: Welcome Back, Ce'Line!
slides.text:
It has been three weeks. I am so glad you are here! 🎉
First, a quick look back. Then two new skills: word problems and the theme of a story.

notes.do: Before class: laptop open to this class lesson (code 9110), small whiteboard and 2 markers, a highlighter, 8 index cards (4 say ADD on green, 4 say SUBTRACT on orange), scrap paper and a pencil, and her printed Packet for Lesson 4. Sit side by side so she can tap and type herself.
notes.say: Welcome back! We had a long break, so today we warm up first. Then you learn two new things. You are going to do great.
notes.ask: How was your break? What was the best part?
notes.listen: Any answer. Smile, keep it short (1–2 minutes), and let her talk. This lesson is about confidence first.

slides.title: What do you remember?
slides.text: Before the break, you followed Theo on his hike and his camping trip. You also worked with big numbers.
prompts: Tell me one thing about your break.

notes.do: 2–3 minutes. She answers out loud in full sentences. Do not correct yet; just listen for what she kept.
notes.ask: Who is Mia? What did Theo use to find the way when the sign was gone?
notes.listen: Mia is Theo's little sister. Theo used his compass and the trail map. If she remembers neither, that is fine: the next two slides review it.

slides.title: Number skills from Weeks 1–3
slides.text: Work on paper, then type.

items.q: Round 368 to the nearest ten: ____
items.why: The ones digit is 8. 5 or more rounds up. 368 rounds to 370.
items.no: Look at the ones digit. 5 or more rounds up.

items.q: Which sign makes this true? 826 ___ 862
items.why: Hundreds are the same (8). Tens: 2 is less than 6. So 826 < 862.
no: That says 826 is bigger. Compare the tens: 2 tens and 6 tens.
= means the same. These numbers are not the same.

items.no: Ones first: 6 + 8 = 14. Write 4 and carry 1 ten.
Ones: 2 − 7 needs a borrow. Make it 12 − 7.

notes.do: She works each one on scrap paper first, then types. Praise every correct step out loud.
notes.ask: On 246 + 178: what did you carry, and where did it go?
notes.listen: 370, <, 424, 275. If she gets 314 for the addition she did not carry; if she gets 325 for the subtraction she took the small digit from the big one. Fix it on the whiteboard in 1 minute and move on; today's word problems use these skills again.

slides.title: Story skills from Weeks 1–3
slides.text: Think about Theo's hike and his camping trip.

items.q: Theo hiked on a misty morning, up the trail to Lookout Peak. That is the story's …
items.why: Setting is where and when a story happens: the trail, a misty morning.
no: A character is a person or animal, like Theo.
The conflict is the problem. This sentence tells where and when.

items.q: The trail sign was gone, and Theo did not know which way to go. The problem in a story is called the ____.
items.why: The problem a character faces is the conflict.
items.no: It is a Week 2 word. It starts with c-o-n.

items.q: How did Theo solve his problem?
choices: He turned around and went home.
He used his compass and his map.
He sat down and waited for someone to help him.
items.why: Theo used the compass and the map to find north. That is the resolution.
no: He thought about turning back, but he did not.
No. Theo solved the problem all on his own.

items.q: “FIRST, they pitched the tent. ____, Theo gathered branches.” Type the missing order word.
items.why: Next (or then) shows the order. Words like these are transition words.
items.no: Use an order word like first, next, then or last.

notes.do: She reads each one out loud before she answers.
notes.ask: What is the beginning, middle and end of Theo's camping trip?
notes.listen: Beginning: they pack and Mia gets to come. Middle: tent, fire, chili. End: dishes in the stream and the stars. If she cannot say it, tell it in three sentences and have her repeat it. Today's story happens at that same campfire.

slides.title: Math words for today
slides.text: Tap each card to flip it. Read the word and the meaning out loud.

words.meaning: A math problem told as a story.
words.example: “Ali has 5 pens. He gets 3 more. How many pens now?” is a word problem.

words.meaning: A word in a word problem that tells you to add or subtract.
words.example: Left is a clue word. It tells me to subtract.

words.meaning: The whole amount after you add everything.
words.example: 136 books and 285 books make a total of 421 books.

words.meaning: A close, smart guess. You round first, then add or subtract.
Makes sense. It is close to what you expect.

notes.do: She reads each card aloud, then says the meaning in her own words.
notes.say: These five words are the tools for word problems. You will type some of them from memory later.
notes.ask: What is the difference between an estimate and the exact answer?
notes.listen: An estimate is close, made with round numbers. The exact answer is the real answer. Both matter: the estimate checks the exact answer.

slides.title: Clue words tell you what to do
slides.text: A word problem is a math story. The clue words tell you to add or subtract.

steps.text: Add clue words: in all, altogether, total, sum, both.
“The library has 136 picture books and 285 chapter books. How many books in all?”
In all means add. 136 + 285 = 421 books.
Subtract clue words: left, remain, how many more, difference.
“The library has 400 bookmarks. Kids took 162. How many are left?”
Left means subtract. 400 − 162 = 238 bookmarks.

slides.tip: Find the clue word first. Then decide: add or subtract?

notes.do: Click the steps one at a time. She highlights the clue word on a scrap-paper copy of each story. Work 136 + 285 and 400 − 162 on the whiteboard together, with her saying each step.
notes.say: Adding and subtracting is not the hard part. You already know how. The hard part is choosing. The clue word chooses for you.
notes.ask: In 400 − 162, the ones are 0 − 2. What do we do?
notes.listen: Borrow. 400 has no tens, so she borrows from the hundreds first: 3 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones. 10 − 2 = 8, 9 − 6 = 3, 3 − 1 = 2: 238. If she freezes, show it with the whiteboard, step by step.

slides.title: Add or subtract?
slides.text: Tap a card. Then tap the right box.

items.text: How many pets in all?
items.why: In all asks for the total. Add.
items.hint: Is it asking for the whole amount?

items.text: How many cookies are left?
items.why: Left means some went away. Subtract.

items.text: What is the total cost?
items.why: Total means put it all together. Add.

items.text: How many more seats do we need?
items.why: How many more asks for the gap. Subtract.
items.hint: It asks for the gap between two numbers.

items.text: How many stickers altogether?
items.why: Altogether means all together. Add.
items.hint: All together means the whole amount.

items.text: How many apples remain?
items.why: Remain means what is still there. Subtract.
items.hint: Remain means what is still there after some are gone.

items.text: What is the difference between the two scores?
items.why: Difference is the answer when you subtract.

items.text: How many books did both girls read?
items.why: Both puts two amounts together. Add.

slides.done: In all, total, altogether, both: add. Left, remain, how many more, difference: subtract.

notes.do: Hand her the 8 index cards first: she sorts the paper cards into ADD and SUBTRACT piles, then does it on screen.
notes.ask: Why is “how many more” a subtract clue, even though it says “more”?
notes.listen: It asks for the gap between two numbers. “More” tricks a lot of students into adding. If she puts it in Add, have her find the gap between 5 and 8 with her fingers: 3, which is 8 − 5.

slides.title: Be a word problem detective
slides.text: Find the clue word. Decide. Then solve on paper.

items.q: The pet shop had 341 fish. It sold 156 fish. How many fish are left? Add or subtract? Type add or subtract.
items.why: The clue words ask what is left or the gap, so you subtract.
items.no: Find the clue word first. Does it ask for a total, or for what is left or the gap?

items.q: The pet shop had 341 fish. It sold 156 fish. How many fish are left?
items.why: The clue word means subtract. 341 − 156 = 185 fish.
items.no: Subtract 341 − 156. Start with the ones. Borrow when the top digit is too small.

items.q: Rosa's team picked 167 apples. Kim's team picked 258 apples. How many apples did they pick altogether?
items.why: The clue word means add. 167 + 258 = 425 apples.
items.no: Add 167 + 258. Line up the ones. Regroup when a column makes 10 or more.

notes.do: She reads each problem out loud, puts her finger on the clue word, and says “add” or “subtract” BEFORE she touches the pencil.
notes.say: Detective steps: read it, find the clue word, decide, then solve.
notes.ask: What is the clue word in the apple problem?
notes.listen: subtract; 185; altogether, 425. If she types 497 for the fish, she added: point back to “left.” If she types 215, she took the small digit from the big digit in each column: redo it with borrowing on the whiteboard.

slides.title: Estimate: round first
slides.text: An estimate is a close, smart guess. Round each number to the nearest hundred. Then add or subtract.

steps.text: Estimate 238 + 451.
238: the tens digit is 3. Less than 5, so round down to 200.
451: the tens digit is 5. 5 or more, so round up to 500.
It works for subtracting too. 612 − 389: 600 − 400 = 200.

slides.tip: To round to the nearest hundred, look at the tens digit.

notes.do: Draw a number line from 200 to 300 on the whiteboard. Mark 238 and ask which hundred it is closer to. Then do 451 between 400 and 500.
notes.say: Estimating is fast. Round, then do easy math with zeros.
notes.ask: What is the exact answer to 238 + 451? Is it close to 700?
notes.listen: 689. Yes, it is close to 700. That is the point: the estimate tells you about how big the answer should be.

slides.title: Round and estimate
slides.text: Look at the tens digit. Then round.

items.q: Round 274 to the nearest hundred: ____
items.why: Look at the tens digit: 7. 5 or more rounds up. So 274 rounds to 300.
items.no: Look at the tens digit. 5 or more rounds up. Less than 5 rounds down.
items.hint: 274 is between 200 and 300. Which is it closer to?

items.q: Round 639 to the nearest hundred: ____
items.why: Look at the tens digit: 3. Less than 5 rounds down. So 639 rounds to 600.
items.no: Look at the tens digit. 5 or more rounds up. Less than 5 rounds down.
items.hint: 639 is between 600 and 700. Which is it closer to?

items.q: Round each number to the nearest hundred. Then add. Estimate 326 + 481: ____
items.no: Round first: 326 → ?, 481 → ?. Then add the round numbers.

items.q: Round each number to the nearest hundred. Then subtract. Estimate 715 − 292: ____
items.no: Round first: 715 → ?, 292 → ?. Then subtract the round numbers.

notes.do: She says the tens digit out loud before every answer.
notes.ask: For 715 − 292: why does 292 round up to 300?
notes.listen: 300, 600, 800, 400. The tens digit of 292 is 9, and 9 is 5 or more, so it rounds up. If she rounds 274 to 270, she rounded to the nearest ten: say, “Hundreds today. Look at the tens digit.”

slides.title: Is my answer reasonable?
slides.text: A reasonable answer is close to your estimate. Use the estimate to check your work.

steps.text: Ana got 769. That is close to 800. ✅ Reasonable.
Ben got 65. That is way too small. ❌ He subtracted instead of adding.
Another check: when you add, the answer is bigger than both numbers. When you take some away, the answer is smaller than the start.

slides.tip: If your answer is far from the estimate, go back and check.

notes.do: She solves 352 + 417 on paper first, to see 769 for herself.
notes.say: Your estimate is your alarm. If the answer is far away, the alarm rings.
notes.ask: Why can't the answer to an “in all” problem be smaller than the numbers you started with?
notes.listen: Because adding puts things together, so you get more. If she says it can, show 3 cards plus 2 cards on the table: 5, more than either pile.

slides.title: Does it make sense?
slides.text: Estimate first. Then choose.

items.q: Estimate first: 409 + 288 is about 400 + 300 = 700. Which answer is reasonable?
items.why: 409 + 288 = 697. It is close to the estimate, 700.
no: 121 is what you get if you subtract. This problem adds.
6,970 is about ten times too big. It is not close to 700.

items.q: A school has 512 students. 238 ride the bus home. How many students do not ride the bus?
items.why: Some students go on the bus, so subtract: 512 − 238 = 274. Estimate: 500 − 200 = 300. 274 is close.
no: 750 is 512 + 238. But the answer must be smaller than 512, because some students are on the bus.
326 came from taking the small digit from the big digit in each column. 2 − 8 needs a borrow.

notes.do: She says the estimate out loud first. For the bus problem, she does 512 − 238 on paper.
notes.ask: Which wrong answer would the estimate catch right away?
notes.listen: 697, then 274. 121 and 6,970 are far from 700; 750 is bigger than 512, which cannot happen when some students leave. 326 is a borrowing mistake: the estimate does not catch it, so she has to check her work.

slides.title: Math check
slides.text: On your own. Clue word, estimate, solve, check.

items.q: A bakery made 430 muffins. It sold 276 muffins. How many muffins are left?
items.why: The clue word means subtract. 430 − 276 = 154 muffins.
items.no: Subtract 430 − 276. Start with the ones. Borrow when the top digit is too small.

items.q: Round each number to the nearest hundred. Then subtract. Estimate 430 − 276: ____
items.no: Round first: 430 → ?, 276 → ?. Then subtract the round numbers.

items.q: Jamal read 186 pages in May and 247 pages in June. How many pages did he read in all?
items.why: The clue word means add. 186 + 247 = 433 pages.
items.no: Add 186 + 247. Line up the ones. Regroup when a column makes 10 or more.

notes.do: Hands off. She works alone on paper and types. Write down her first answers.
notes.listen: 154, 100, 433. All three right on the first try means the math half of the Pathways Week 4 retake is in reach. A wrong operation means 2 more minutes with the ADD/SUBTRACT cards at the start of next week.

slides.title: Reading words for today
slides.text: Tap each card to flip it. Read the word and the meaning out loud.

words.meaning: The big lesson about life that a story teaches.
words.example: The theme of a story can be “Never give up.”

words.meaning: The lesson at the end of a fable.
words.example: The moral of a fable can be “Slow and steady wins the race.”

words.meaning: Being caring and giving to other people.
words.example: Sharing your snack is an act of kindness.

notes.do: She reads each card aloud and gives one example from her own life for “lesson” and “kindness.”
notes.say: Every story tells what happens. Many stories also teach a lesson. That lesson is the theme.
notes.ask: What is a lesson you learned the hard way?
notes.listen: Any real example (“I learned to save my work”). Connect it: a story's theme is the same kind of lesson.

slides.title: The Last S'more, Part 1
slides.text: Back at the campfire, Theo has a choice to make. Read it with Mr. Jonathan.

visual.text: After dinner, Theo and Mia roasted marshmallows over the campfire. There was only ONE marshmallow left in the bag. Theo reached for it first. His fingers were almost touching it when he glanced at Mia. She was staring at the empty bag with a small, disappointed frown, trying hard not to show it.

prompts: How does Mia feel? What clue tells you?
What do you think Theo will do?
starters: If I were Theo, I would …

notes.do: Read it together: you read the first sentence, she reads the next, and so on. 5 minutes in all.
notes.say: The story never says how Mia feels. We figure it out from clues. That is called inferring.
notes.ask: Why does the author spend so many words on one little marshmallow?
notes.listen: Mia wants it too but is trying to hide it (clue: the small, disappointed frown). Something important is about to happen. Accept any reasonable prediction with a “because.”

visual.text: After dinner, Theo and Mia roasted marshmallows over the campfire. There was only ONE marshmallow left in the bag. Theo reached for it first. His fingers were almost touching it when he glanced at Mia. She was staring at the empty bag with a small, disappointed frown, trying hard not to show it.

items.q: What was Mia staring at?
items.why: Mia was staring at the empty bag.
items.no: Look at the last sentence of the story.

items.q: Which clue shows how Mia feels?
items.why: The frown is a clue. Mia wants the marshmallow too, but she tries not to show it.
no: That tells when, not how Mia feels.
That tells where, not how Mia feels.
That is about Theo, not how Mia feels.

items.q: Who reached for the last marshmallow first?
items.why: Theo reached for it first.
items.no: Look at the third sentence.

notes.do: She answers on her own, then points to the words in the story that prove it.
notes.ask: Point to the words that prove your answer.
notes.listen: the empty bag; the frown; Theo. Praise “pointing to the proof” every time. That habit wins points on the Pathways retake.

slides.title: The Last S'more, Part 2
slides.text: Now see what Theo decides.

visual.text: Theo's hand hovered over the marshmallow. He could hear his stomach thinking about how good it would taste. But he kept looking at Mia's face. He remembered how she'd begged for weeks to come on this trip. Slowly, Theo picked up the marshmallow and broke it in half. “Here,” he said, holding out the bigger piece to Mia. “Race you to see who can make theirs melt the gooiest.”

steps.text: Theo could have kept the whole marshmallow. Nobody would stop him.
Theo chose to break it in half and give Mia the bigger piece.
He made it a fun race, so Mia would not feel bad.

slides.tip: When a character makes a choice, ask: What does this teach me?

notes.do: She reads Part 2 out loud. Then click the steps one at a time.
notes.say: This is the big moment of the story. Theo had a choice.
notes.ask: Why did Theo give Mia the bigger piece, and not just half?
notes.listen: He was really thinking about her feelings. He remembered how much she wanted to come on the trip.

visual.text: Theo's hand hovered over the marshmallow. He could hear his stomach thinking about how good it would taste. But he kept looking at Mia's face. He remembered how she'd begged for weeks to come on this trip. Slowly, Theo picked up the marshmallow and broke it in half. “Here,” he said, holding out the bigger piece to Mia. “Race you to see who can make theirs melt the gooiest.”

items.q: What did Theo do with the marshmallow? He ____ it in half.
items.why: Theo broke it in half.
items.no: Look for the word right before “in half.”

items.q: What clue shows Theo really cared about Mia's feelings?
choices: He gave Mia the bigger piece.
items.why: He gave Mia the bigger piece. That shows he put her first.
no: That shows Theo wanted it himself.
Slowly shows he was thinking, but the bigger piece shows he cared.
That tells when, not what Theo felt.

items.q: Theo remembered something about Mia. She had ____ for weeks to come on this trip.
items.why: Mia had begged for weeks. Theo remembered how much this trip meant to her.
items.no: Look at the fourth sentence.

notes.do: She answers, then says why in one sentence.
notes.listen: broke; the bigger piece; begged. If she picks the stomach, ask: “Does wanting it yourself show you care about Mia?”

slides.title: Plot or theme?
slides.text: Plot is what happens. Theme is the lesson about life.

steps.text: Plot: Theo shared the last marshmallow with Mia.
To find the theme, ask: What did the character learn? What does the story teach me?
Theme: Being kind to someone you love can feel better than keeping it all.
A theme is a whole idea, not one name. “Theo” is not a theme.
A theme must fit the story. “Always listen to your stomach” does not fit. Theo did the opposite!

slides.tip: Plot tells about the story. Theme tells about life.

notes.do: Draw a T-chart on the whiteboard: PLOT | THEME. Write each step's example in the right column as you click.
notes.say: The plot is only about Theo. The theme is about everybody, even you and me.
notes.ask: Say the theme in your own words.
notes.listen: Something like “Sharing with people you love feels good” or “Kindness matters more than a treat.” Any version about kindness or sharing is right. If she retells the plot, ask: “What does this teach YOU?”

slides.title: Plot or theme?
slides.text: Tap a card. Then tap the right box.

items.text: Theo and Mia roast marshmallows.
items.why: This tells what happens.
items.hint: Is it only about Theo and Mia?

items.text: Sharing can make a moment better for everyone.
items.why: This is a lesson about life.
items.hint: Could this be true for anyone?

items.text: Only one marshmallow is left.
items.why: This tells what happens.
items.hint: Is it something that happens in the story?

items.text: Thinking about others' feelings is a kind choice.
items.why: This is a lesson about life.
items.hint: Is this a lesson for everyone?

items.text: Theo breaks the marshmallow in half.
items.why: This tells what happens.
items.hint: Is it an action in the story?

items.text: Kindness can matter more than a treat.
items.why: This is a lesson about life.

slides.done: Plot is what happens. Theme is the lesson. Great sorting!

notes.do: She reads each card out loud before she taps it.
notes.ask: How can you tell a theme card fast?
notes.listen: Theme cards do not name Theo or Mia; they could be true for anybody.

slides.title: Find the moral
slides.text: A fable is a short story that teaches a lesson.

visual.text:
The Ant and the Grasshopper
All summer, the ant carried food to her home. The grasshopper sang and played in the sun. “Why work so hard?” he asked. Then winter came. The ant had plenty of food. The grasshopper had nothing to eat.

items.q: What is the moral of this fable?
choices: All summer long, the grasshopper sang and played in the sun.
Work hard now, and you will be ready later.
items.why: The ant worked and was ready for winter. The lesson: work hard now, and you will be ready later.
no: That is plot. It tells what happens.
That does not fit. The grasshopper had nothing to eat!
A theme is a whole idea, not one name.

items.q: The lesson at the end of a fable is called the ____.
items.why: It is the moral.
items.no: It is one of today's reading words. It starts with m.

items.q: “The ant had plenty of food.” Is this the plot or the theme? Type plot or theme.
items.why: It tells what happens, so it is plot.
items.no: Plot is what happens. Theme is a lesson about life.

notes.do: On her own. She reads the fable out loud first.
notes.listen: Work hard now…; moral; plot. If she picks “Singing is better,” ask: “What happened to the grasshopper in winter? Does that sound better?”

slides.title: Two big skills
slides.text: You came back strong today! 💪

steps.text: Word problems: find the clue word, then add or subtract.
Estimate: round to the nearest hundred. Is the answer reasonable?
Theme: ask, “What lesson does this story teach?”

slides.tip: Tonight: the after-class lesson. It ends with Show What You Know. Aim for 85.

notes.do: Open the course page together and read the task list, one day at a time. Point to the two Pathways Week 4 retakes (Friday and Monday).
notes.say: Tonight, just the after-class lesson. A little each day after that.
notes.ask: Tell me the add clue words and the subtract clue words without looking.
notes.listen: In all, altogether, total, both. Left, remain, how many more, difference. Then one sentence: what is a theme?

slides.title: Solve It, Estimate It: On Your Own
slides.text:
Welcome back! Now you practice what you learned in class.
Keep paper and a pencil next to you.

slides.title: Explain it out loud
slides.text: Say these to a grown-up, or say them out loud to yourself.
prompts: Name 2 clue words that mean add. Name 2 that mean subtract.
What is the theme of “The Last S'more”?
starters: Add words are … Subtract words are …

slides.title: Review your words
slides.text: Say the meaning out loud first. Then flip the card to check.

words.meaning: A math problem told as a story.
words.example: “Ali has 5 pens. He gets 3 more. How many pens now?” is a word problem.

words.meaning: A word in a word problem that tells you to add or subtract.
words.example: Left is a clue word. It tells me to subtract.

words.meaning: The whole amount after you add everything.
words.example: 136 books and 285 books make a total of 421 books.

words.meaning: A close, smart guess. You round first, then add or subtract.
Makes sense. It is close to what you expect.
The big lesson about life that a story teaches.
words.example: The theme of a story can be “Never give up.”

words.meaning: The lesson at the end of a fable.
words.example: The moral of a fable can be “Slow and steady wins the race.”

slides.title: Detective steps
slides.text: Do these steps on every word problem.

steps.text: 1. Read the whole problem.
2. Find the clue word.
3. Decide: add or subtract?
4. Estimate: round to the nearest hundred.
5. Solve on paper. 6. Check: is it close to the estimate?

slides.tip: Theme: ask, “What lesson does this story teach?”

slides.title: Add or subtract?
slides.text: Find the clue word first.

items.q: A farm had 364 hens. 127 hens went to a new barn. How many hens remain? Add or subtract? Type add or subtract.
items.why: The clue words ask what is left or the gap, so you subtract.
items.no: Find the clue word first. Does it ask for a total, or for what is left or the gap?

items.q: Lila sold 215 tickets on Friday and 187 on Saturday. How many tickets did she sell in all? Add or subtract? Type add or subtract.
items.why: The clue words ask for the total, so you add.
items.no: Find the clue word first. Does it ask for a total, or for what is left or the gap?

items.q: Which clue words tell you to subtract?
items.why: How many more asks for the gap between two numbers. Subtract.
no: Sum means add.
Altogether means add.
In all means add.

slides.title: Round and estimate
slides.text: Look at the tens digit.

items.q: Round 583 to the nearest hundred: ____
items.why: Look at the tens digit: 8. 5 or more rounds up. So 583 rounds to 600.
items.no: Look at the tens digit. 5 or more rounds up. Less than 5 rounds down.
items.hint: 583 is between 500 and 600. Which is it closer to?

items.q: Round each number to the nearest hundred. Then add. Estimate 247 + 318: ____
items.no: Round first: 247 → ?, 318 → ?. Then add the round numbers.

items.q: Round each number to the nearest hundred. Then subtract. Estimate 806 − 391: ____
items.no: Round first: 806 → ?, 391 → ?. Then subtract the round numbers.

slides.title: Solve it
slides.text: Solve on paper first. Then type the number.

items.q: The zoo had 254 visitors in the morning. 179 more came in the afternoon. How many visitors in all?
items.why: The clue word means add. 254 + 179 = 433 visitors.
items.no: Add 254 + 179. Line up the ones. Regroup when a column makes 10 or more.

items.q: A box had 500 crayons. The class used 264. How many crayons are left?
items.why: The clue word means subtract. 500 − 264 = 236 crayons.
items.no: Subtract 500 − 264. Start with the ones. Borrow when the top digit is too small.

items.q: Mia found 145 shells. Theo found 213 shells. How many more shells did Theo find?
items.why: The clue word means subtract. 213 − 145 = 68 more shells.

slides.title: Leo and the Kite
slides.text: Read the story. Then answer.

visual.text: Leo borrowed his friend Max's kite. A big wind blew. The kite hit a tree and tore. Leo hid the kite under his bed. All week, his tummy felt bad. On Friday, Leo told Max the truth. “Thank you for telling me,” Max said. They fixed the kite together.

items.q: Where did Leo hide the kite?
items.why: Leo hid it under his bed.
items.no: Look at the fourth sentence.

items.q: What is the theme of this story?
choices: Leo hid the kite under his bed.
Kites can tear in the wind.
Telling the truth is better than hiding a mistake.
You should never borrow anything from a friend, not even a kite.
items.why: Leo felt bad when he hid it. He felt better when he told the truth. That is the theme.
no: That is plot. It tells what happens.
That is a small detail, not the big lesson.
That does not fit. Max was glad Leo told him.

items.q: “Leo told Max the truth.” Is this the plot or the theme? Type plot or theme.
items.why: It tells what happens, so it is plot.
items.no: Plot is what happens. Theme is a lesson about life.

slides.title: Sam's Swim
slides.text: Read the story. Then answer.

visual.text: Sam could not swim across the pool. On Monday, he sank and swallowed water. He wanted to quit. His coach said, “Try one more time.” Sam practiced every day. On Friday, Sam swam all the way across! Everyone cheered.

items.q: Why did Sam want to quit?
choices: The other kids at the pool laughed at him.
items.why: On Monday, Sam sank and swallowed water.
no: The coach said, “Try one more time.” That is kind, not yelling.
The story does not say anyone laughed.

items.q: What is the theme of this story?
choices: On Friday, Sam swam all the way across the pool.
If you keep trying, you can get better.
items.why: Sam kept practicing and did it. The lesson: keep trying.
no: That is plot. It tells what happens.
That does not fit. Sam learned to swim!
A theme is a whole idea, not one name.

items.q: Sam's lesson in 2 words: Don't give ____.
items.why: Don't give up!
items.no: What do you say to a friend who wants to quit?

Kai's wagon wheel kept falling off. He wanted to fix it all by himself. He tried for an hour. The wheel fell off again and again. At last, Kai asked his grandpa for help. Together, they fixed it in five minutes.

teacher.objective: Ce'Line comes back from the three-week break with a quick review of Weeks 1–3 (rounding, comparing, regrouping; setting, conflict and resolution, sequence). Then she solves one-step addition and subtraction word problems by finding the clue word (in all, altogether, total, both / left, remain, how many more, difference), estimates sums and differences by rounding to the nearest hundred, and uses the estimate to decide if an answer is reasonable. In reading, she reads “The Last S'more” (Pathways Week 4), infers Mia's feelings from clues, tells plot from theme, and states the theme of a story in a whole sentence.
materials: The class lesson on the laptop (teacher code 9110)
8 index cards: 4 green cards that say ADD, 4 orange cards that say SUBTRACT (for the clue-word sort)
A highlighter, scrap paper and a pencil
Her printed Packet for Lesson 4 (2 pages) to take home

plan.do: Class slides 1–2. Warm hello, one thing about her break, what she remembers about Theo and regrouping.
Class slides 3–4. Rounding to tens, comparing, regrouping on paper; then setting, conflict, resolution and sequence. Fix only what is quick; note anything that slipped.
Class slide 5. She reads the 5 cards aloud and says each meaning in her own words.
Class slides 6–7. The library examples on the whiteboard (136 + 285, 400 − 162). She sorts the paper ADD/SUBTRACT cards, then the screen sort.
Class slide 8. Finger on the clue word, say add or subtract, then solve on paper.
Class slides 9–10. Number line 200 to 300 on the whiteboard; round to the nearest hundred by the tens digit; four tries.
Class slides 11–12. Estimate as an alarm; adding makes it bigger, taking away makes it smaller.
Class slide 13 on her own. Write down her first answers (154, 100, 433).
Class slide 14. Theme, lesson, moral, kindness, with one example of her own.
Class slides 15–18. Read Part 1 together, infer Mia's feeling from the frown, point to proof; read Part 2 and Theo's choice.
Class slides 19–20. T-chart on the whiteboard; she says the theme in her own words; plot-or-theme sort.
Class slide 21. The fable on her own: moral, the word moral, plot or theme.
Class slide 22. Say the clue words; open the course page and read the task list one day at a time.

watch: Picking the operation from the numbers, not the words: she may add every time. Before she writes anything, she puts her finger on the clue word and says “add” or “subtract.” No clue word said, no pencil.
“How many more”: the word “more” pulls students toward adding. Show the gap with fingers (5 and 8: 3 more) and write 8 − 5.
Borrowing: when the top digit is smaller (2 − 8), the common mistake is to flip it (8 − 2). Say: “Top digit too small? Borrow.” With zeros (400 − 162), borrow from the hundreds first.
Rounding to the wrong place: she learned tens in Week 1. Today is hundreds: she circles the tens digit, then decides up or down.
Plot vs. theme: she may retell what happened. Ask: “Does it name Theo? Then it is plot. What does it teach YOU?”
One-word themes: “kindness” is the key word, but on the packet she writes a whole sentence (the Pathways retake asks for the key word, and both are right).
Confidence after the break: praise every correct step out loud. If she freezes, give the first step and let her finish.

packet_key.answer: Clue: how many more. Subtract. 231 − 147 = 84 more pinecones
372 + 419 = 791. Yes, 791 is close to the estimate of 800, so it is reasonable.
Any whole sentence like: It is okay to ask for help. / Asking for help can make a hard job easy.
Any whole sentence about sharing or kindness, like: Sharing with someone you love can feel better than keeping something for yourself.

teacher.notes: For you only: this is her first lesson after the three-week break, so slides 2–4 tell you what she kept from Weeks 1–3. If rounding or regrouping slipped badly, spend 3 extra minutes there and shorten the reading exit ticket (the after-class lesson repeats the theme work). Tonight she does the after-class lesson; it ends with Show What You Know (8 questions, 3 different sets for retakes, she needs 85, so 7 of 8). If she scores under 85, look at the Formspree missed list: a wrong operation means 5 minutes with the ADD/SUBTRACT cards at the start of Lesson 5; a borrowing mistake means 3 subtraction problems on the whiteboard with her saying each step; a missed theme means one more short story with the T-chart. Her retakes are Pathways Week 4 Reading on Friday and Pathways Week 4 Math on Monday (aim 85). Lesson 5 next Tuesday is the Unit 1 Checkpoint (Weeks 1–4), so everything today comes back next week.

tasks: Tuesday (after class): do the after-class lesson. It ends with Show What You Know. Aim for 85.
Wednesday: do the Practice set. Circle the clue word on paper before you solve.
Thursday: print the Packet and do page 1.
Friday: do Pathways Week 4 Reading (The Last S'more). Plot is what happens. Theme is the lesson. Aim for 85. If it is locked, type 1111.
Saturday: do page 2 of the Packet. Then do the Practice set again. You get new questions.
Monday: do Pathways Week 4 Math. Find the clue word, estimate, then solve on paper. Aim for 85. If it is locked, type 1111.
Optional: Science Week 4 or Social Studies Week 4, on your own (see Also do).
